lesson.title: The Chain Rule Hiding Inside Every y-Term
lesson.summary: On equations that mix powers, products, and sums of x and y, the chain rule on y-terms combines with the product rule to differentiate the whole equation correctly.
lesson.body:
You now know the core rule: for any expression g(y) built out of y, d/dx[g(y)] = g'(y) times dy/dx, because y(x) is the inner function and the chain rule always attaches a copy of the inner function's derivative. The next step is combining that rule with everything else you already know, especially the product rule, on equations where x and y appear tangled together in the same term.

The folium of Descartes, x^3 + y^3 = 6xy, is the classic example, because it needs both rules at once. Differentiate every term with respect to x. On the left, d/dx[x^3] = 3x^2, and d/dx[y^3] = 3y^2 (dy/dx) by the chain rule described above. On the right, 6xy is a product of x and y(x), so it needs the product rule: d/dx[6xy] = 6[x (dy/dx) + y]. Putting it together:

3x^2 + 3y^2 (dy/dx) = 6x (dy/dx) + 6y

Now collect every term containing dy/dx on one side and everything else on the other: 3y^2 (dy/dx) - 6x (dy/dx) = 6y - 3x^2. Factor out dy/dx: (dy/dx)(3y^2 - 6x) = 6y - 3x^2. Divide: dy/dx = (6y - 3x^2)/(3y^2 - 6x), which simplifies to (2y - x^2)/(y^2 - 2x).

Check this at the point (3, 3), which does lie on the curve since 3^3 + 3^3 = 27 + 27 = 54 and 6(3)(3) = 54 as well. Plugging in: dy/dx = (2(3) - 3^2)/(3^2 - 2(3)) = (6 - 9)/(9 - 6) = -3/3 = -1. The tangent line to the folium of Descartes at (3, 3) has slope -1, a well-known result for this curve, and one you now know how to reproduce from scratch by combining the chain rule on y^3 with the product rule on 6xy.
